title: Linux Pipes and I/O Redirection
markdown:
# Linux Pipes and I/O Redirection

Every command in Linux communicates through three channels: **standard input** (where it reads data from), **standard output** (where it writes normal results), and **standard error** (where it writes errors). By default, these channels connect to your keyboard and terminal screen. **I/O redirection** lets you reconnect them — sending output to files, reading input from files, and separating errors from normal results. **Pipes** go further, connecting the output of one command directly to the input of the next to build multi-step data processing pipelines in a single line.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/operators-summary.svg)

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Redirect `stdout` to a file with `>` and `>>`
- Feed file contents into a command with `<`
- Capture error messages separately with `2>` and `2>&1`
- Chain commands together using pipes (`|`)
- Split output to both the terminal and a file with `tee`

## The Scenario: Routing Pipeline Output at `Poridhi.io`

The analytics platform at `Poridhi.io` runs data jobs that produce a mix of normal output and error messages. Your job is to route each stream correctly: errors to an error log, summaries to a report file, and critical data visible on screen while also being saved.

To practice, we will create a set of sample log files and build the pipeline step by step.

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `pipeline/data/access.log` | Sample access log for filtering and pipeline exercises |
| `pipeline/data/mixed.log` | Log file with mixed normal and error entries |
| `pipeline/reports/` | Directory where all output and error files will be saved |

## Part 1: The Three Data Streams

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/Standard-streams.svg)

Every Linux process works with three standard channels:

| Stream | File Descriptor | Default | Redirected with |
|--------|----------------|---------|-----------------|
| `stdin` | `0` | Keyboard | `<` |
| `stdout` | `1` | Terminal | `>`, `>>` |
| `stderr` | `2` | Terminal | `2>`, `2>&1` |

The file descriptors are numbers the shell uses to identify each channel. When you write `2>&1`, you're telling the shell: "send file descriptor 2 (`stderr`) to wherever file descriptor 1 (`stdout`) is currently going." The rest of this lab puts each of these to use.

## Part 2: Setting Up the Environment

### Step 1: Create the Working Directories

```bash
mkdir -p pipeline/data
mkdir -p pipeline/reports
```

### Step 2: Create Sample Data Files

```bash
cat > pipeline/data/access.log << 'EOF'
192.168.1.10 GET /api/users 200 14ms
192.168.1.11 GET /api/orders 200 22ms
192.168.1.12 POST /api/upload 500 891ms
192.168.1.10 GET /api/users 200 12ms
192.168.1.13 DELETE /api/session 403 8ms
192.168.1.14 GET /api/reports 200 31ms
192.168.1.12 POST /api/upload 500 903ms
192.168.1.15 GET /api/users 200 10ms
EOF
```

```bash
cat > pipeline/data/mixed.log << 'EOF'
INFO  service started successfully
ERROR failed to connect to database
INFO  health check passed
ERROR disk usage above 90%
INFO  request processed
ERROR failed to connect to database
INFO  cache warmed up
EOF
```

Verify both files were created:

```bash
cat pipeline/data/access.log
cat pipeline/data/mixed.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image.png)

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-1.png)

## Part 3: Output Redirection (`>` and `>>`)

The `>` operator redirects `stdout` to a file. If the file exists, it is **overwritten**. If it doesn't exist, it is **created**. The `>>` operator **appends** to the file instead of overwriting it.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/output-redirection.svg)

### Step 1: Save Command Output to a File

Extract all 500 errors from the access log and save them to a report file:

```bash
grep "500" pipeline/data/access.log > pipeline/reports/errors.txt
cat pipeline/reports/errors.txt
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-2.png)

Run the same command again and check the line count — the file is replaced, not extended:

```bash
grep "500" pipeline/data/access.log > pipeline/reports/errors.txt
wc -l pipeline/reports/errors.txt
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-3.png)

### Step 2: Append to a File with `>>`

Add a timestamp to the bottom of the report without overwriting it:

```bash
echo "Report generated: $(date)" >> pipeline/reports/errors.txt
cat pipeline/reports/errors.txt
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-4.png)

**Why it matters**: Use `>` when you want a clean file each run (like a daily report that replaces the previous one). Use `>>` when you need to accumulate entries over time (like a running log).

## Part 4: Input and Error Redirection

### Step 1: Feed a File into a Command with `<`

Use `wc` to count log lines by feeding the file through stdin:

```bash
wc -l < pipeline/data/access.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-5.png)

Compare this with passing the filename as an argument:

```bash
wc -l pipeline/data/access.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-6.png)

With `<`, `wc` reads from stdin and prints just the number. With a filename argument, it prints the number and the filename. The difference matters when chaining commands that only read from stdin.

### Step 2: Capture Errors Separately with `2>`

Run a command that produces both normal output and an error:

```bash
ls pipeline/data /nonexistent-directory
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-7.png)

This lists the contents of `pipeline/data` successfully but also prints an error for the nonexistent directory.

Both the file listing and the error print to the terminal. Now capture only the error:

```bash
ls pipeline/data /nonexistent-directory 2> pipeline/reports/ls-errors.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-8.png)

Normal output still prints to the terminal. Here `2>` redirects only the error stream to a file, leaving normal output unaffected.

Verify the error was captured separately:

```bash
cat pipeline/reports/ls-errors.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-9.png)

### Step 3: Capture Both Streams Together with `2>&1`

Send all output — both stdout and stderr — into one file:

```bash
ls pipeline/data /nonexistent-directory > pipeline/reports/combined.log 2>&1
cat pipeline/reports/combined.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-10.png)

To discard all output when you don't need it:

```bash
ls pipeline/data /nonexistent-directory > /dev/null 2>&1
```

Here, both normal output and errors are sent to `/dev/null`, a special file that discards all data written to it. This is useful in scripts where you only care about the exit status of a command and want to suppress all output. `/dev/null` is a special Linux device file that discards anything written to it.

We can check the `dev/null` device:

```bash
ls -l /dev/null
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-11.png)

But we cannot read from it as anything written to it is discarded permanently:

```bash
cat /dev/null
```

> **Note:** Order matters. Always write `> file 2>&1`, not `2>&1 > file`. The shell processes redirections left to right — the second form redirects stderr to the terminal before stdout is changed to the file.

**Why it matters**: In production scripts, separating stdout and stderr lets you monitor normal output without error noise, and capture errors without losing the normal output.

## Part 5: Chaining Commands with Pipes (`|`)

A pipe connects the `stdout` of one command to the `stdin` of the next. No intermediate files needed — data flows through memory.

### Step 1: Basic Pipe

Count how many requests returned a 200 status:

```bash
grep "200" pipeline/data/access.log | wc -l
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-12.png)

Here, `grep` filters the log for lines containing "200", and `wc -l` counts those lines. The pipe (`|`) connects them directly.

Find which endpoints appear most frequently:

```bash
awk '{print $3}' pipeline/data/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-13.png)

**Each command does one job:** `awk` extracts the endpoint column, `sort` groups identical values, `uniq -c` counts them, and `sort -rn` ranks by count. Here, `-rn` means "reverse numeric" sort — highest counts first.

### Step 2: Build a Multi-Stage Error Pipeline

Extract all ERROR lines from the mixed log, deduplicate them, and count unique errors:

```bash
grep "ERROR" pipeline/data/mixed.log | sort | uniq
```

```bash
grep "ERROR" pipeline/data/mixed.log | sort | uniq | wc -l
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-14.png)

**Why it matters**: Pipes let you build complex data transformations from simple, focused tools without writing intermediate files. Each command does one thing — the shell connects them.

## Part 6: Splitting Output with `tee`

`tee` reads from stdin and writes to **both** stdout and a file simultaneously — named after the T-shaped pipe fitting that splits flow in two directions. This is useful when you want to see output on the terminal while also saving it. 

### Step 1: Log and Display at the Same Time

Run the error pipeline from Part 5 and save the results while watching them on screen:

```bash
grep "ERROR" pipeline/data/mixed.log | sort | uniq | tee pipeline/reports/error-summary.txt
```

The errors print to the terminal and are saved to the file in one pass. Verify:

```bash
cat pipeline/reports/error-summary.txt
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-15.png)

### Step 2: Capture an Intermediate Stage

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/tee-command.svg)

Use `tee` in the middle of a pipeline to capture data at a specific point without breaking the flow:

```bash
grep "ERROR" pipeline/data/mixed.log | tee pipeline/reports/raw-errors.txt | sort | uniq | wc -l
```

This saves the raw (unsorted, undeduped) error lines to a file while the pipeline continues and prints only the final count to the terminal. Both happen in a single pass.

We can check the raw errors captured:

```bash
cat pipeline/reports/raw-errors.txt
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2010/images/image-16.png)

**Why it matters**: `tee` is essential in long pipelines where you need to inspect or archive data at an intermediate stage without splitting the pipeline or running it twice.

## Conclusion

In this lab, we built a complete data routing system using Linux's core I/O operators. Each operator solves a specific problem:

- `>` and `>>` — save command output to files, overwriting or appending
- `<` — feed file contents to commands that read from stdin
- `2>` and `2>&1` — separate or combine error and normal output streams
- `|` — chain commands into data processing pipelines without intermediate files
- `tee` — split a stream to both the terminal and a file simultaneously

These operators compose naturally. A real production script might use `grep`, `|`, `tee`, `>>`, and `2>` all in a single line — and now you have the foundation to read and write exactly that.
